title: Isaiah 53 — The fourth Servant Song: the suffering servant

paragraphs.text: מִ֥י הֶאֱמִ֖ין לִשְׁמֻעָתֵ֑נוּ וּזְר֥וֹעַ יְהוָ֖ה עַל־מִ֥י נִגְלָֽתָה׃

i18n.en: Who has believed what we have heard? And the arm of YHWH — to whom has it been laid bare?
i18n.he: מִ֥י הֶאֱמִ֖ין לִשְׁמֻעָתֵ֑נוּ וּזְר֥וֹעַ יְהוָ֖ה עַל־מִ֥י נִגְלָֽתָה׃

notes.official:
The fourth Servant Song proper opens not here but at 52:13–15, whose *rām wᵉniśśāʾ* “exalted and lifted up” — said of the servant — deliberately echoes the throne “high and lifted up” of the inaugural vision (Isa 6:1; see the overlay entry throne-ram-venissa-isaiah). Chapter 53 is the body of that song, spoken by a “we” who report what they once thought and now confess. This source file segments at 53:1; the 52:13 head is noted here rather than re-segmented.

*mî heʾĕmîn li-šmuʿāṯēnû* “Who has believed what we have heard?” and *ûzᵉrôaʿ YHWH* “the arm of YHWH” open the confession. The “arm of YHWH” is the standard anthropomorphic idiom for divine power in action (cf. the Exodus “outstretched arm,” Deut 26:8), rendered literally; the point that the servant is where that power is “laid bare” (*niḡlāṯāh*) is the song’s opening paradox (Blenkinsopp, *Isaiah 40–55*, AB 19A, 2002). The verse is taken up in the New Testament reception (John 12:38; Rom 10:16), noted as part of the text’s later history, not its sense.

paragraphs.text: וַיַּ֨עַל כַּיּוֹנֵ֜ק לְפָנָ֗יו וְכַשֹּׁ֙רֶשׁ֙ מֵאֶ֣רֶץ צִיָּ֔ה לֹא־תֹ֥אַר ל֖וֹ וְלֹ֣א הָדָ֑ר וְנִרְאֵ֥הוּ וְלֹֽא־מַרְאֶ֖ה וְנֶחְמְדֵֽהוּ׃

i18n.en: He grew up like a sapling before him, like a root out of parched ground. He had no form and no splendor that we should look at him, no appearance that we should find him desirable.
i18n.he: וַיַּ֨עַל כַּיּוֹנֵ֜ק לְפָנָ֗יו וְכַשֹּׁ֙רֶשׁ֙ מֵאֶ֣רֶץ צִיָּ֔ה לֹא־תֹ֥אַר ל֖וֹ וְלֹ֣א הָדָ֑ר וְנִרְאֵ֥הוּ וְלֹֽא־מַרְאֶ֖ה וְנֶחְמְדֵֽהוּ׃

notes.official: *lᵉpānāyw* “before him” is left ambiguous, as in the Hebrew: the servant grew up either before YHWH (in his sight) or before the beholders, and the translation does not resolve it. The plant-imagery — *yônēq* “sapling / sucker” and *šōreš* “root” out of *ʾereṣ ṣiyyāh* “parched ground” — pictures an unpromising, unregarded growth: no *tōʾar* “form” and no *hāḏār* “splendor” to draw the eye (Goldingay & Payne, ICC *Isaiah 40–55*).

paragraphs.text: נִבְזֶה֙ וַחֲדַ֣ל אִישִׁ֔ים אִ֥ישׁ מַכְאֹב֖וֹת וִיד֣וּעַ חֹ֑לִי וּכְמַסְתֵּ֤ר פָּנִים֙ מִמֶּ֔נּוּ נִבְזֶ֖ה וְלֹ֥א חֲשַׁבְנֻֽהוּ׃

i18n.en: He was despised and shunned by men, a man of pains and acquainted with sickness; and like one from whom faces are hidden, he was despised, and we held him of no account.
i18n.he: נִבְזֶה֙ וַחֲדַ֣ל אִישִׁ֔ים אִ֥ישׁ מַכְאֹב֖וֹת וִיד֣וּעַ חֹ֑לִי וּכְמַסְתֵּ֤ר פָּנִים֙ מִמֶּ֔נּוּ נִבְזֶ֖ה וְלֹ֥א חֲשַׁבְנֻֽהוּ׃

notes.official:
*wa-ḥăḏal ʾîšîm* is a crux: *ḥāḏēl* “ceasing, lacking” with *ʾîšîm* “men” can mean “forsaken/rejected by men,” “shunned by men,” or “lacking in men (esteem).” The translation reads “shunned by men,” with the “forsaken/rejected of men” of ASV/JPS an equivalent.

The servant is *ʾîš maḵʾōḇôṯ wîḏûaʿ ḥŏlî* “a man of pains and acquainted with sickness.” The disease-vocabulary (*maḵʾōḇôṯ* “pains,” *ḥŏlî* “sickness”) runs on into v 4 and is rendered plainly as physical affliction; whether literal illness or a metaphor for suffering is a matter of the song’s imagery, not the lexicon (Blenkinsopp; North, *The Suffering Servant in Deutero-Isaiah*). The figure is unnamed throughout — the governing question of the servant’s identity is treated at 53:11.

paragraphs.text: אָכֵ֤ן חֳלָיֵ֙נוּ֙ ה֣וּא נָשָׂ֔א וּמַכְאֹבֵ֖ינוּ סְבָלָ֑ם וַאֲנַ֣חְנוּ חֲשַׁבְנֻ֔הוּ נָג֛וּעַ מֻכֵּ֥ה אֱלֹהִ֖ים וּמְעֻנֶּֽה׃

i18n.en: Surely it was our sicknesses that he bore, and our pains that he carried; yet we ourselves accounted him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted.
i18n.he: אָכֵ֤ן חֳלָיֵ֙נוּ֙ ה֣וּא נָשָׂ֔א וּמַכְאֹבֵ֖ינוּ סְבָלָ֑ם וַאֲנַ֣חְנוּ חֲשַׁבְנֻ֔הוּ נָג֛וּעַ מֻכֵּ֥ה אֱלֹהִ֖ים וּמְעֻנֶּֽה׃

notes.official:
*ʾāḵēn ḥŏlāyēnû hûʾ nāśāʾ* “Surely it was our sicknesses that he bore” turns the confession: the “we” now see that the servant carried what was theirs. *nāśāʾ* “bore” and *sāḇal* “carried” are the vicarious-bearing verbs that recur at 53:11–12 (see the overlay entry nasa-sabal-vicarious-bearing-isaiah); the substitutionary sense — one bearing what belongs to others — is developed in the reception but is not overloaded onto the plain verbs here.

The verse’s second half reports a *mistaken* judgment: *wa-ʾănaḥnû ḥăšaḇnuhû nāḡûaʿ mukkēh ʾĕlōhîm ûmᵉʿunneh* “yet we ourselves accounted him stricken, struck down by God, and afflicted.” This is what the onlookers *wrongly* thought — that his suffering marked him as one God had punished — and 53:5 immediately corrects it (“but he was pierced because of *our* transgressions”).

Because the clause voices a misperception the text overturns, *ʾĕlōhîm* here is rendered “God” at the standard surface and the corpus convention “the Elohim” is deliberately *not* applied (see the overlay entry elohim-as-god-observers-53-4-isaiah): to read “struck down by the Elohim” would import a lens-claim onto the one line the poem stages precisely in order to reject it. *mukkēh ʾĕlōhîm* is best taken as a divine-passive / superlative-of-severity (“God-smitten,” a stricken man), a report of appearance rather than a datum about agency (Goldingay & Payne). The verse is later applied to Jesus’ healings at Matt 8:17, noted as reception.

paragraphs.text: וְהוּא֙ מְחֹלָ֣ל מִפְּשָׁעֵ֔נוּ מְדֻכָּ֖א מֵעֲוֺנֹתֵ֑ינוּ מוּסַ֤ר שְׁלוֹמֵ֙נוּ֙ עָלָ֔יו וּבַחֲבֻרָת֖וֹ נִרְפָּא־לָֽנוּ׃

i18n.en: But he was pierced because of our transgressions, crushed because of our iniquities; the discipline that brought us peace was upon him, and by his wounds we were healed.
i18n.he: וְהוּא֙ מְחֹלָ֣ל מִפְּשָׁעֵ֔נוּ מְדֻכָּ֖א מֵעֲוֺנֹתֵ֑ינוּ מוּסַ֤ר שְׁלוֹמֵ֙נוּ֙ עָלָ֔יו וּבַחֲבֻרָת֖וֹ נִרְפָּא־לָֽנוּ׃

notes.official:
*wᵉhûʾ mᵉḥōlāl mippᵉšāʿēnû mᵉḏukkāʾ mēʿăwōnōṯênû* “But he was pierced because of our transgressions, crushed because of our iniquities.” *mᵉḥōlāl* is a Pual of *ḥll* I “to pierce, bore through, fatally wound” (hence “pierced,” with ASV “wounded” an equivalent); a minority derives it from *ḥll* II “profane, defile,” which the translation declines (see the overlay entry mecholal-pierced-isaiah). The prepositional *min* (*mippᵉšāʿēnû*, *mēʿăwōnōṯênû*) is causal — “because of / on account of our transgressions and iniquities” — not agential; the servant suffers *for* the people’s wrongs, and the sin-pair *pešaʿ* / *ʿāwōn* is cross-corpus keyword vocabulary (see avon-iniquity-cross-corpus-keyword).

*mûsar šᵉlômēnû ʿālāyw* “the discipline that brought us peace was upon him,” and *ûḇaḥăḇurāṯô nirpāʾ-lānû* “by his wounds we were healed.” The vicarious-atonement reading these lines carry in later interpretation — the servant’s suffering as reparation for others — is the chapter’s most contested theological freight; per the house register it is set out as a reading, hedged, not asserted as the verse’s settled meaning (Blenkinsopp; Baltzer, *Deutero-Isaiah*, Hermeneia). The half-verse is quoted at 1 Pet 2:24 (“by his wounds you have been healed”).

paragraphs.text: כֻּלָּ֙נוּ֙ כַּצֹּ֣אן תָּעִ֔ינוּ אִ֥ישׁ לְדַרְכּ֖וֹ פָּנִ֑ינוּ וַֽיהוָה֙ הִפְגִּ֣יעַ בּ֔וֹ אֵ֖ת עֲוֺ֥ן כֻּלָּֽנוּ׃

i18n.en: All of us have strayed like sheep; each has turned to his own way; and YHWH has laid upon him the iniquity of us all.
i18n.he: כֻּלָּ֙נוּ֙ כַּצֹּ֣אן תָּעִ֔ינוּ אִ֥ישׁ לְדַרְכּ֖וֹ פָּנִ֑ינוּ וַֽיהוָה֙ הִפְגִּ֣יעַ בּ֔וֹ אֵ֖ת עֲוֺ֥ן כֻּלָּֽנוּ׃

notes.official:
*kullānû kaṣṣōʾn tāʿînû* “all of us have strayed like sheep” — the confessing “we” admit the fault was theirs. *wa-YHWH hip̄gîaʿ bô ʾēṯ ʿăwōn kullānû* “and YHWH has laid upon him the iniquity of us all”: the Hiphil of *pāḡaʿ* means “cause to fall/strike upon, make [something] meet [someone]” — YHWH makes the people’s iniquity converge on the servant (see the overlay entry paga-lay-on-intercede-isaiah). The same root closes the poem at 53:12 (*yap̄gîaʿ* “make intercession”), framing the servant’s role between the iniquity laid on him and the intercession he makes — a deliberate inclusio.

*ʿāwōn* “iniquity” (also 53:5, 53:11) is one of the three principal Hebrew sin-lexemes and is governed by the central keyword entry avon-iniquity-cross-corpus-keyword, whose own rationale names these verses; the standard “iniquity” is retained. The straying-sheep image is picked up at 1 Pet 2:25.

paragraphs.text: נִגַּ֨שׂ וְה֣וּא נַעֲנֶה֮ וְלֹ֣א יִפְתַּח־פִּיו֒ כַּשֶּׂה֙ לַטֶּ֣בַח יוּבָ֔ל וּכְרָחֵ֕ל לִפְנֵ֥י גֹזְזֶ֖יהָ נֶאֱלָ֑מָה וְלֹ֥א יִפְתַּ֖ח פִּֽיו׃

i18n.en: He was oppressed, and he was afflicted, yet he would not open his mouth; like a lamb led to the slaughter, like a ewe fallen silent before her shearers, he would not open his mouth.
i18n.he: נִגַּ֨שׂ וְה֣וּא נַעֲנֶה֮ וְלֹ֣א יִפְתַּח־פִּיו֒ כַּשֶּׂה֙ לַטֶּ֣בַח יוּבָ֔ל וּכְרָחֵ֕ל לִפְנֵ֥י גֹזְזֶ֖יהָ נֶאֱלָ֑מָה וְלֹ֥א יִפְתַּ֖ח פִּֽיו׃

notes.official:
*niggaś wᵉhûʾ naʿăneh* “he was oppressed, and he was afflicted”: *naʿăneh* is read as a passive (Niphal of *ʿnh*, parallel to *niggaś* “oppressed”), with the reflexive “he humbled himself” of ASV/JPS an equivalent the translation does not take. The servant’s silence — *wᵉlōʾ yip̄taḥ pîw* “he would not open his mouth” — is doubled around two similes: *kaśśeh laṭṭeḇaḥ yûḇāl* “like a lamb led to the slaughter,” and *ûḵᵉrāḥēl … neʾĕlāmāh* “like a ewe fallen silent before her shearers.”

The sacrificial resonance of the lamb-simile is developed in the reception, not asserted here; this is the passage the Ethiopian official is reading (from the Old Greek) when Philip expounds it at Acts 8:32–33 — the New Testament’s most explicit application of the song to Jesus, noted as reception history (North).

paragraphs.text: מֵעֹ֤צֶר וּמִמִּשְׁפָּט֙ לֻקָּ֔ח וְאֶת־דּוֹר֖וֹ מִ֣י יְשׂוֹחֵ֑חַ כִּ֤י נִגְזַר֙ מֵאֶ֣רֶץ חַיִּ֔ים מִפֶּ֥שַׁע עַמִּ֖י נֶ֥גַע לָֽמוֹ׃

i18n.en: By restraint and by judgment he was taken away; and as for his generation, who gave it a thought — that he was cut off from the land of the living, stricken for the transgression of my people?
i18n.he: מֵעֹ֤צֶר וּמִמִּשְׁפָּט֙ לֻקָּ֔ח וְאֶת־דּוֹר֖וֹ מִ֣י יְשׂוֹחֵ֑חַ כִּ֤י נִגְזַר֙ מֵאֶ֣רֶץ חַיִּ֔ים מִפֶּ֥שַׁע עַמִּ֖י נֶ֥גַע לָֽמוֹ׃

notes.official:
A dense crux-verse. *mēʿōṣer ûmimmišpāṭ luqqāḥ* “by restraint and by judgment he was taken away”: *ʿōṣer* is coercion / detention / oppression and *mišpāṭ* a legal judgment, the *min* most likely instrumental (“through”); some read it privatively (“taken away *from* oppression,” i.e. released by death). *wᵉʾeṯ-dôrô mî yᵉśôḥēaḥ* “and as for his generation, who gave it a thought?” turns on *śîaḥ* “muse, consider, declare.”

*kî niḡzar mēʾereṣ ḥayyîm* “that he was cut off from the land of the living” states the servant’s death plainly (*gzr* “cut off, sever”; see the overlay entry nigzar-cut-off-isaiah) — the death the following verse then buries. *mippešaʿ ʿammî neḡaʿ lāmô* “stricken for the transgression of my people”: *lāmô* is formally plural (“to them”) but is widely read as a singular (“to him,” the servant), and the translation leaves the number unresolved, as the Hebrew does. The form bears on the identity question — a plural “to them” has been read as evidence for a corporate servant — and is flagged rather than decided (Goldingay & Payne; Blenkinsopp). The Acts 8 citation continues into this verse.

paragraphs.text: וַיִּתֵּ֤ן אֶת־רְשָׁעִים֙ קִבְר֔וֹ וְאֶת־עָשִׁ֖יר בְּמֹתָ֑יו עַ֚ל לֹא־חָמָ֣ס עָשָׂ֔ה וְלֹ֥א מִרְמָ֖ה בְּפִֽיו׃

i18n.en: His grave was set with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death, though he had done no violence and no deceit was in his mouth.
i18n.he: וַיִּתֵּ֤ן אֶת־רְשָׁעִים֙ קִבְר֔וֹ וְאֶת־עָשִׁ֖יר בְּמֹתָ֑יו עַ֚ל לֹא־חָמָ֣ס עָשָׂ֔ה וְלֹ֥א מִרְמָ֖ה בְּפִֽיו׃

notes.official:
*wayyittēn ʾeṯ-rᵉšāʿîm qiḇrô wᵉʾeṯ-ʿāšîr bᵉmōṯāyw* “his grave was set with the wicked, and with a rich man in his death.” The impersonal *wayyittēn* (“one assigned”) is rendered as an English passive. *ʿāšîr* “a rich man” stands in parallel with *rᵉšāʿîm* “the wicked” — a dishonorable burial among the guilty; the translation keeps the Masoretic “rich,” though the awkward parallelism has prompted proposed emendations (e.g. to a synonym of “wicked”), which are declined.

*bᵉmōṯāyw* is formally a plural, “in his deaths,” rendered as a singular “in his death” (a plural of intensity or abstraction; see the overlay entry bemotayw-death-burial-isaiah); the Great Isaiah Scroll (1QIsaᵃ) reads instead *bāmāṯô* “his burial-mound / high place,” a variant noted for the reader’s audit. The servant’s innocence is asserted — *lōʾ-ḥāmās ʿāśāh* “he had done no violence,” *lōʾ mirmāh bᵉp̄îw* “no deceit in his mouth” — the latter quoted at 1 Pet 2:22.

paragraphs.text: וַיהוָ֞ה חָפֵ֤ץ דַּכְּאוֹ֙ הֶֽחֱלִ֔י אִם־תָּשִׂ֤ים אָשָׁם֙ נַפְשׁ֔וֹ יִרְאֶ֥ה זֶ֖רַע יַאֲרִ֣יךְ יָמִ֑ים וְחֵ֥פֶץ יְהוָ֖ה בְּיָד֥וֹ יִצְלָֽח׃

i18n.en: Yet YHWH was pleased to crush him; he laid sickness upon him. If his life is set down as a guilt-offering, he shall see offspring, he shall prolong his days, and the purpose of YHWH shall prosper in his hand.
i18n.he: וַיהוָ֞ה חָפֵ֤ץ דַּכְּאוֹ֙ הֶֽחֱלִ֔י אִם־תָּשִׂ֤ים אָשָׁם֙ נַפְשׁ֔וֹ יִרְאֶ֥ה זֶ֖רַע יַאֲרִ֣יךְ יָמִ֑ים וְחֵ֥פֶץ יְהוָ֖ה בְּיָד֥וֹ יִצְלָֽח׃

notes.official:
*wa-YHWH ḥāp̄ēṣ dakkᵉʾô* “yet YHWH was pleased to crush him” — the poem’s hardest line, referring the servant’s suffering to YHWH’s own purpose. *heḥĕlî* is taken as a Hiphil of *ḥlh* “he made him sick” (continuing the disease-thread of 53:3–4).

*ʾim-tāśîm ʾāšām nap̄šô* “if his life is set down as a guilt-offering.” *ʾāšām* is the Levitical guilt- / reparation-offering (Lev 5–7), governed as a cross-corpus term by the central entry ashem-asham-guilt-bearing-vocabulary; here a *human life* (*nep̄eš*) is what is offered, and the subject of *tāśîm* is uncertain (“if you [YHWH] make…,” or “if his life is made…”). The translation uses an impersonal passive and does not resolve the subject (see the overlay entry asham-nefesh-guilt-offering-53-10-isaiah). The application of the cultic reparation-offering to a person is the interpretive core of the verse and is set out, hedged, in the reception rather than asserted in the line (Blenkinsopp; Baltzer).

*yirʾeh zeraʿ yaʾărîḵ yāmîm* “he shall see offspring, he shall prolong his days”: vindication beyond the death just described. *zeraʿ* “seed / offspring” resonates with the *zeraʿ qōḏeš* “holy seed” remnant of Isa 6:13 (overlay entry zera-qodesh-holy-seed-isaiah) — a surviving seed-line after catastrophe — though the phrase here carries no *qōḏeš* and the link is thematic, not lexical.

paragraphs.text: מֵעֲמַ֤ל נַפְשׁוֹ֙ יִרְאֶ֣ה יִשְׂבָּ֔ע בְּדַעְתּ֗וֹ יַצְדִּ֥יק צַדִּ֛יק עַבְדִּ֖י לָֽרַבִּ֑ים וַעֲוֺנֹתָ֖ם ה֥וּא יִסְבֹּֽל׃

i18n.en: Out of the toil of his soul he shall see; he shall be satisfied. By his knowledge the righteous one, my servant, shall bring the many to righteousness, and their iniquities he himself shall carry.
i18n.he: מֵעֲמַ֤ל נַפְשׁוֹ֙ יִרְאֶ֣ה יִשְׂבָּ֔ע בְּדַעְתּ֗וֹ יַצְדִּ֥יק צַדִּ֛יק עַבְדִּ֖י לָֽרַבִּ֑ים וַעֲוֺנֹתָ֖ם ה֥וּא יִסְבֹּֽל׃

notes.official:
Two cruxes and the governing question of the song. (1) A major text-critical variant: the Masoretic *mēʿămal nap̄šô yirʾeh yiśbāʿ* “out of the toil of his soul he shall see; he shall be satisfied” has no object for “see,” and both Great Isaiah Scrolls (1QIsaᵃ, 1QIsaᵇ) together with the Old Greek read *yirʾeh ʾôr* “he shall see **light**” — an object that materially strengthens the vindication-after-death (resurrection) reading. The translation retains the Masoretic text and discloses the “light” variant here for the reader’s audit (see the overlay entry yireh-or-dss-lxx-variant-53-11-isaiah); the variant is adopted by several modern critical versions (Blenkinsopp; Goldingay & Payne).

(2) *bᵉḏaʿtô yaṣdîq ṣaddîq ʿaḇdî lārabbîm* — the word order permits “the righteous one, my servant, shall bring the many to righteousness,” or the attributive “my righteous servant shall justify the many” (ASV). The translation reads the former; *yaṣdîq* is the causative “make/declare righteous, justify,” and *ʿăwōnōṯām* “their iniquities” he “carries” (*sāḇal*, the bearing-verb of 53:4).

*ʿaḇdî* “my servant” — explicit here — is the figure who has run un-named through the whole song, and its referent is the chapter’s governing crux. The mainstream Jewish reading takes the servant as corporate Israel or a faithful remnant (grounded in Isa 49:3 “you are my servant, Israel,” and the medieval commentators). A second reading takes an individual — a suffering prophet, or Deutero-Isaiah himself (Duhm’s isolation of the four Servant Songs). The Christian reading takes the servant as an individual messiah who suffers vicariously, and this is the reading the New Testament develops in its reception of the song (Acts 8:32–35; 1 Pet 2:22–25). Some scholarship also notes a broader comparative resonance with the pattern of a righteous sufferer humiliated and then vindicated. The Hebrew names no referent, and the translation identifies none: per the house register these are set out as comparative and critical readings, all hedged, and no identification is imported into the text (see the overlay entry eved-servant-identity-isaiah; North surveys the history of interpretation).

paragraphs.text: לָכֵ֞ן אֲחַלֶּק־ל֣וֹ בָרַבִּ֗ים וְאֶת־עֲצוּמִים֮ יְחַלֵּ֣ק שָׁלָל֒ תַּ֗חַת אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֶעֱרָ֤ה לַמָּ֙וֶת֙ נַפְשׁ֔וֹ וְאֶת־פֹּשְׁעִ֖ים נִמְנָ֑ה וְהוּא֙ חֵטְא־רַבִּ֣ים נָשָׂ֔א וְלַפֹּשְׁעִ֖ים יַפְגִּֽיעַ׃ (ס)

i18n.en: Therefore I will give him a share among the many, and with the mighty he shall divide the spoil; because he poured out his life to death and was numbered with transgressors — yet he himself bore the sin of many and made intercession for the transgressors.
i18n.he: לָכֵ֞ן אֲחַלֶּק־ל֣וֹ בָרַבִּ֗ים וְאֶת־עֲצוּמִים֮ יְחַלֵּ֣ק שָׁלָל֒ תַּ֗חַת אֲשֶׁ֨ר הֶעֱרָ֤ה לַמָּ֙וֶת֙ נַפְשׁ֔וֹ וְאֶת־פֹּשְׁעִ֖ים נִמְנָ֑ה וְהוּא֙ חֵטְא־רַבִּ֣ים נָשָׂ֔א וְלַפֹּשְׁעִ֖ים יַפְגִּֽיעַ׃ (ס)

notes.official:
*lāḵēn ʾăḥalleq-lô ḇārabbîm* “therefore I will give him a share among the many, and with the *ʿăṣûmîm* “the mighty” he shall divide spoil” — a victor’s reward, whose exact scope (“a portion among the many/great” vs “the many as his portion”) is debated (Goldingay & Payne). *taḥaṯ ʾăšer* “because / in return for the fact that” is the substitution-and-recompense formula governed by the central entry tachat-substitution-formula, whose rationale already reaches to Isaiah 53.

The grounds follow: *heʿĕrāh lammāweṯ nap̄šô* “he poured out his life to death,” *wᵉʾeṯ-pōšᵉʿîm nimnāh* “and was numbered with transgressors” (quoted at Luke 22:37), *wᵉhûʾ ḥēṭʾ-rabbîm nāśāʾ* “yet he himself bore the sin of many” (*nāśāʾ*, the bearing-verb of 53:4), *wᵉlappōšᵉʿîm yap̄gîaʿ* “and made intercession for the transgressors.” This last is the Hiphil of *pāḡaʿ* that opened the poem’s central movement at 53:6 (“laid on him the iniquity”): the root that made iniquity strike the servant now has him interposing for the guilty — the closing term of the inclusio (see paga-lay-on-intercede-isaiah).
